## Set Up

Libraries used

-   [ggstatsplot](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ggstatsplot/index.html) Extends ggplot2 by automatically adding information-rich statistical test results (p-values, Bayes factors, effect sizes) directly onto information-dense data visualizations.
-   [ggdist](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ggdist/index.html) Provides a flexible set of specialized ggplot2 geoms and stats designed for visualizing distributions, uncertainty intervals, and Bayesian posterior densities (like half-eye and dotplots).
-   [see](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/see/index.html) Serves as the visual engine for the easystats ecosystem, offering clean, publication-ready themes and custom ggplot2 geoms to easily plot complex statistical model outputs.
-   [tidyverse](https://tidyverse.org/) An opinionated collection of core data science packages (like dplyr, ggplot2, and tidyr) designed to work seamlessly together for clean data manipulation, exploration, and visualization.
-   [skimr](https://docs.ropensci.org/skimr/) Provides an elegant, frictionless summary function that produces a beautifully structured console overview of data types, missing value rates, and inline histogram sparklines for a dataset.
-   [naniar](http://naniar.njtierney.com/) Offers a specialized suite of structures and visualizations to look at patterns, percentages, and systemic structures of missing data (NA values) without altering your baseline rows.
-   [scales](https://scales.r-lib.org/) Controls the underlying mathematical transformation, axis formatting, and labeling mechanics of plots, allowing you to easily map numbers to clean currency, percentages, or logarithmic scales.
-   [arrow](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/arrow/index.html) Provides an interface to Apache Arrow, enabling ultra-fast read/write data pipelines, out-of-memory computations, and seamless querying of massive parquet file portfolios.
-   [patchwork](https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com/) Makes combining multiple separate ggplot2 charts into cohesive, multi-panel layouts or slide grids as simple as using basic arithmetic operators like + and /.
-   [GGally](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGally/index.html) Extends ggplot2 by combining multiple columns into compound visual layouts, such as pairwise correlation matrix grids (pairs plots) and parallel coordinate plots.
-   [glue](https://tidyverse.r-universe.dev/articles/glue/glue.html) Replicates the smooth developer experience of Python’s f-strings in R, allowing you to cleanly evaluate expressions and parse variables directly inside text strings using curly braces {}.
-   [ggpubr](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ggpubr/index.html) Wraps complex ggplot2 commands into simpler functions optimized for creating publication-ready, clean statistical charts for research papers and academic panels.
-   [treemapify](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/treemapify/vignettes/introduction-to-treemapify.html) Adds custom tiles and text-fitting geoms to ggplot2 to easily build nested, variable-area treemaps for visualizing categorical concentration and financial value distributions.
-   [vcd](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/vcd/index.html) Provides a highly structured suite of statistical tools and custom visual plots (like mosaic and association plots) designed specifically to evaluate contingency tables and categorical data associations.

## Data Cleaning

### Clean up of data, data type conversion and new variable creation

-   Convert all categorical values with acronym into readable label
-   Remove the 2 rows of data where vehicle age and age driving license is null
-   Impute Median to vehicle age and mode to fuel type
-   We also created indicator called underwriting profit to identify which portfolios are losses.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Create function to calculate mode
calc_mode <- function(x) {
  distinct_values <- unique(x[!is.na(x)])
  distinct_values[which.max(tabulate(match(x, distinct_values)))]
}

# Pre-calculate the mode safely outside the pipeline to unblock the compiler
fuel_mode <- calc_mode(df$fuel_type)

df_transformed <- df %>%
  mutate(
    # All the factor like variables
    policy_type = case_when(
      policy_type == "TP"     ~ "Basic Third-Party",
      policy_type == "TPG"    ~ "Third-Party with Glass Cov",
      policy_type == "CC"     ~ "Third-Party with two or more Cov",
      policy_type == "COMP_E" ~ "Comprehensive with Excess",
      policy_type == "COMP_N" ~ "Comprehensive without Excess",
      TRUE                    ~ "Others"
    ),
    policy_status = case_when(
      policy_status == 'A' ~ "Active",
      policy_status == 'C' ~ "Cancelled",
      TRUE                 ~ "Others"
    ),
    business_type = case_when(
      business_type == 'NB' ~ "New_Business",
      business_type == 'P' ~ "Portfolio",
      TRUE                 ~ "Others"
    ),
    payment_frequency = case_when(
      payment_frequency == 'A' ~ "Annual",
      payment_frequency == 'S' ~ "Semi-Annual",
      payment_frequency == 'Q' ~ "Quarterly",
      TRUE                     ~ "Others"
    ),
    bonus_score = case_when(
      bonus_score == 'G' ~ "Positive",
      bonus_score == 'N' ~ "Neutral",
      bonus_score == 'B' ~ "Negative",
      TRUE                 ~ "Others"
    ),
    fuel_type = case_when(
      fuel_type == 'D' ~ "Diesel",
      fuel_type == 'G' ~ "Gasoline",
      is.na(fuel_type) ~ NA_character_,
      TRUE                 ~ "Others"
    ),
    municipality_type = case_when(
      municipality_type == 'I' ~ "Inland",
      municipality_type == 'C' ~ "Coastal",
      municipality_type == 'IS' ~ "Islands",
```

### 3. Premiums from 2022 to 2024

-   This is to perform confirmatory data analysis that there is a change in distribution amongst the various product over the years

-   Where Null Hypothesis: The distribution of total premium is identical across all three years Alternative Hypothesis: The distribution of total premium is not identical across all three years; at least one year's premium distribution stochastically dominates

-   We also observed that there are extreme values in total premiums, hence a log is applied to the y axis to help observe the full range of premiums more easily

### Create function


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot_policy_distribution <- function(data, target_policy, target_metric = "total_premium") {
  
  # 1. Dynamically filter and prepare data based on function arguments
  # We use .data[[target_metric]] to allow passing the column name as a string
  plot_data <- data %>%
    filter(
      policy_type == target_policy,
      .data[[target_metric]] > 0
    ) %>%
    mutate(year = factor(year))
  
  # Determine dynamic text for labels
  metric_label <- gsub("_", " ", target_metric) %>% tools::toTitleCase()
  
  # 2. Safe Statistical Check
  unique_years <- unique(plot_data$year)
  
  if (length(unique_years) > 1) {
    # Dynamically build formula: target_metric ~ year
    formula_obj <- as.formula(paste(target_metric, "~ year"))
    stat_test   <- kruskal.test(formula_obj, data = plot_data)
    
    stat_label  <- paste0(
      "Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = ", round(stat_test$statistic, 2),
      ", df = ", stat_test$parameter,
      ", p-value = ", scales::scientific(stat_test$p.value, digits = 3)
    )
  } else if (length(unique_years) == 1) {
    stat_label <- paste0("Kruskal-Wallis: Insufficient groups (Only ", unique_years, " data available)")
  } else {
    # If string matching yields 0 rows, print warning and stop to avoid ggplot crash
    warning(paste0("No data found for policy type: '", target_policy, "' with ", metric_label, " > 0."))
    return(NULL)
  }
  
  # 3. Generate the Plot
  p <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = year, y = .data[[target_metric]], fill = year)) +
    
    # The Half-Eye distribution view
    stat_halfeye(
      adjust = 0.5,
      width = 0.6,
      .width = c(0.66, 0.95),
      point_color = "black",
      interval_color = "black",
      alpha = 0.7
    ) +
    
    # Scale and formatting
    scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma(prefix = "$")) +
    scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues", guide = "none") +
    
    # Informative labels that update dynamically based on your inputs
    labs(
      title = paste0(metric_label, " Distribution across Years"),
      subtitle = paste0(target_policy, "\n", stat_label),
      x = "Year",
      y = paste0(metric_label, " (Log Scale)")
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "gray30", size = 10, face = "italic"),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      axis.text = element_text(face = "bold")
    ) +
  coord_flip() 
  return(p)
}


plot_pairwise_matrix <- function(data, target_policy, target_metric = "total_premium") {
  
  # 1. Filter data based on input arguments
  plot_data <- data %>%
    filter(
      policy_type == target_policy,
      .data[[target_metric]] > 0
    ) %>%
    mutate(year = factor(year))
  
  # Clean up the metric name for beautiful axis/title labels
  metric_label <- gsub("_", " ", target_metric) %>% tools::toTitleCase()
  
  # 2. Check if pairwise testing is mathematically possible
  if (length(unique(plot_data$year)) < 2) {
    warning(paste0("Skipping matrix: '", target_policy, "' does not have enough distinct years with data."))
    return(NULL)
  }
  
  # 3. Execute the Pairwise Wilcoxon Test with Holm Adjustment
  wt_result <- pairwise.wilcox.test(
    x = plot_data[[target_metric]], 
    g = plot_data$year,
    p.adjust.method = "holm"
  )
  
  p_matrix <- wt_result$p.value
  
  # Handle edge case where the matrix is completely empty/NULL
  if (all(is.na(p_matrix))) {
    warning(paste0("No valid variance found to compute pairwise shifts for '", target_policy, "'."))
    return(NULL)
  }
  
  # 4. Transform matrix to a tidy long-format dataframe
  p_df_long <- as.data.frame(p_matrix) %>%
    mutate(Group_B = rownames(.)) %>%
    pivot_longer(
      cols = -Group_B, 
      names_to = "Group_A", 
      values_to = "p_val"
    ) %>%
    filter(!is.na(p_val)) %>%
    mutate(
      # Ensure factor matching for explicit manual scale mapping
      is_significant = factor(p_val < 0.05, levels = c("TRUE", "FALSE")),
      p_label = if_else(p_val < 0.001, "p < 0.001", paste0("p = ", round(p_val, 3)))
    )
  
  # 5. Build the Dynamic Matrix Plot
  p <- ggplot(p_df_long, aes(x = Group_A, y = Group_B, fill = is_significant)) +
    geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1.5) +
    geom_text(aes(label = p_label), color = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 4.5) +
    
    # Red/Coral for significant shifts, neutral grey for stagnant periods
    scale_fill_manual(
      values = c("TRUE" = "#2ca02c", "FALSE" = "#7f8c8d"),
      labels = c("TRUE" = "Significant Shift (p < 0.05)", "FALSE" = "No Stat. Difference"),
      name = "Holm Conclusion",
      drop = FALSE 
    ) + 
    
    # FORCE the legend preview boxes to show their true assigned colors manually
    guides(
      fill = guide_legend(
        override.aes = list(fill = c("#2ca02c", "#7f8c8d"))
      )
    ) + 
    
    labs(
      title = paste0("Pairwise Post-Hoc Shifts Matrix (", metric_label, ")"),
      subtitle = paste0(target_policy, "\nWilcoxon Rank-Sum Test (Holm-Adjusted Method)"),
      x = "Baseline Year (Group A)",
      y = "Comparison Year (Group B)"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "gray30", face = "italic", size = 10, margin = margin(b = 10)),
      axis.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
      panel.grid = element_blank(),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.title = element_text(face = "bold")
    )
  
  return(p)
}
```

Function created to ease the coding below. Instead of blue we will use red for claims for the violin plot below. We also remove log in the Y axis as there is less claim variation in price as compared to premiums

```{.r .cell-code}
plot_claims_distribution <- function(data, target_policy, target_metric = "total_incurred") {
  
  # 1. Dynamically filter and prepare data based on function arguments
  # We use .data[[target_metric]] to allow passing the column name as a string
  plot_data <- data %>%
    filter(
      policy_type == target_policy,
      .data[[target_metric]] > 0
    ) %>%
    mutate(year = factor(year))
  
  # Determine dynamic text for labels
  metric_label <- gsub("_", " ", target_metric) %>% tools::toTitleCase()
  
  # 2. Safe Statistical Check
  unique_years <- unique(plot_data$year)
  
  if (length(unique_years) > 1) {
    # Dynamically build formula: target_metric ~ year
    formula_obj <- as.formula(paste(target_metric, "~ year"))
    stat_test   <- kruskal.test(formula_obj, data = plot_data)
    
    stat_label  <- paste0(
      "Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = ", round(stat_test$statistic, 2),
      ", df = ", stat_test$parameter,
      ", p-value = ", scales::scientific(stat_test$p.value, digits = 3)
    )
  } else if (length(unique_years) == 1) {
    stat_label <- paste0("Kruskal-Wallis: Insufficient groups (Only ", unique_years, " data available)")
  } else {
    # If string matching yields 0 rows, print warning and stop to avoid ggplot crash
    warning(paste0("No data found for policy type: '", target_policy, "' with ", metric_label, " > 0."))
    return(NULL)
  }
  
  # 3. Generate the Plot
  p <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = year, y = .data[[target_metric]], fill = year)) +
    
    # The Half-Eye distribution view
    stat_halfeye(
      width = 0.6,
      .width = c(0.66, 0.95),
      point_color = "black",
      interval_color = "black",
      alpha = 0.7
    )  + 
  scale_y_log10(
    limits = c(0.10, 500000), 
    labels = scales::label_dollar(),
    breaks = c(0.10, 1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000, 100000, 500000)
  ) +
    scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Reds", guide = "none") +
    
    # Informative labels that update dynamically based on your inputs
    labs(
      title = paste0(metric_label, " Distribution across Years"),
      subtitle = paste0(target_policy, "\n", stat_label),
      x = "Year",
  y = paste0(metric_label, " (Log Scale)")
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "gray30", size = 10, face = "italic"),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      axis.text = element_text(face = "bold")
    ) +
  coord_flip() 
  return(p)
}
```
